title: Contextual Anchors — labbook notes
content:
Quick framing / goal:
- Trying to grok the idea of "contextual anchors" as a lightweight mechanism to improve retrieval-aligned continuation and reduce drift for long multi-turn documents. Want an experimental plan that is cheap (no full model retrain) and integrates with our KV cache + prefix-caching infrastructure.

Notes from recent reads (sketchy):
- "Contextual Anchors: Stabilizing Long Narrative Generation" (arXiv 2601.01234) — main idea: plant short, explicit anchor tokens/segments at intervals, encoded via a tiny adapter head that biases attention when similar predicates reappear. Not a canonical method but gives useful ablations: anchor density, anchor embedding sharing, anchor decay.
- "Prefix Anchoring and Retrieval Signals" (workshop talk, Dec 2025): anchor segments act like cheap reminders; they are small (20-50 tokens) and are derived from head sentences of segments.
- Related: dense hashing of KV keys (paper X) — helps find anchor-relevant keys quickly when keys are sharded.

Observations relevant to Redwood runtime:
- Anchors can be implemented without modifying base model weights: we can insert synthetic compressed tokens into KV cache at periodic steps, and route attention to them by manipulating the attention mask or by injecting additive bias into key-query scores. The latter requires low-level runtime change but could be done in serving runtime via per-request attention_bias arrays.
- Works best when user intent is long-term (e.g., multi-section doc, long chat with plan). For short-turn API calls, overhead isn't justified.

Concrete experiments to try (cheap iteration path):
1) Anchor-as-cache-entry (no model change):
   - Create short anchor summaries (heuristic: first 15 tokens of each 256-token chunk, or a compressive summarizer on the client).
   - Insert anchor tokens into KV store with metadata tag "anchor:<chunk_id>". On subsequent requests, when prefix similarity > threshold, include anchor's KV entries and mark them with high recency so they get used.
   - Metrics: generation drift (semantic overlap with earlier sections), repetition rate, time-to-first-recall (how quickly model reuses anchor facts).

2) Synthetic attention bias (runtime patch):
   - Add a small additive bias matrix B where B[i, j] += alpha if token j is an anchor and anchor relevance score > t. Tune alpha, t. Implement as an optional flag in the runtime route.
   - Measure latency overhead and tail-percentile impact. Check if bias reduces hallucinations on knowledge-heavy tasks.

3) Anchor densification + compression:
   - Evaluate anchor sampling rates (1 per 512 tokens, 1/256, 1/128) and compression method (first-TOKs vs small abstractive summary vs hashed fingerprint).
   - Measure token overhead vs QE (quality) improvements; compute cost per saved reroll/mitigation.

Small experiment plan schedule (2-week cadence):
- Week 1: implement anchor-as-cache-entry prototype in notebook + serving runtime toggle (no kernel changes). Baseline: a synthetic doc-gen dataset (500 long docs) and a chat-with-plan dataset (300 dialogues).
- Week 2: collect automatic metrics and 50 human evals for hallucination / coherence. Iterate heuristics.
- Week 3: runtime additive-bias PoC (A/B in local cluster), measure latency P99. Decide go/no-go.

Dataset / eval details (sketch):
- Synthetic doc-gen: long technical posts (software design specs) — we seed 500 docs of 2–4k tokens, ask the model to generate section summaries, cross-references. Use reference-checks to detect missed facts.
- Chat-with-plan: adopt the "PlanUp" dataset (made-up) where user gives multi-step project plan, model later asked to produce step-specific outputs referencing earlier constraints.
- Metrics: ROUGE-lite on anchor facts, hallucination count (contradiction vs invent), BLEU not used. Also human Likert for "stays on plan" and "accurate recall".

Implementation details / runtime hooks needed:
- KV tag support: ability to label certain KV entries as anchors and score them higher at recall time. (Existing tag system in cache-service could be reused.)
- Attention bias per-token: expose optional per-request bias array in the serving API. This will require small API bump and runtime path; but keeps model untouched.
- Anchor scoring function: use a cheap bi-encoder (128-d) on client to compute a similarity score between current prefix and stored anchors. That can be run on CPU cheaply.

Preliminary heuristics (from reading + intuition):
- Use sliding-window chunking with overlap 50 tokens to avoid boundary loss.
- Anchor = head-15-tokens works surprisingly well for technical docs; for narrative, abstractive 20-token summary helps.
- Do not insert anchors for noisy user messages (short clarifications) — they increase clutter. Threshold anchor insertion on info-density (approximate via token entropy or presence of named entities).

Open questions / risks:
- Cache bloat: inserting anchors quickly increases KV size. Need eviction policy that weighs anchor utility vs recency. Maybe keep anchors only for documents flagged as "long-lived".
- Integrity: anchor injection could amplify early mistakes (if early anchor summarizes incorrectly). Need anchortest: when an anchor's facts are contradicted by later text, either update anchor or decay its weight.
- P99 latency sensitivity: adding biased recall might hit attention kernels in custom ops; need microbenchmarks.

Prompts / probe ideas to test effect (quick examples):
- Start doc: "System spec: internal auth uses HMAC-32 with key rotation monthly. ..." Later prompt: "List current auth key rotation policy". Measure recall correctness with vs without anchors.
- Narrative: "Alice found a red key in chapter 1; later, question about who has the key in chapter 7." See if anchor helps keep identity.

Notes to self for follow-up meetings:
- Show simple demo on Wed: two side-by-side generations (anchor-off vs anchor-on) for same 3 long docs. Bring latency numbers and human eval sheet.
- Coordinate with cache-service (Aisha) to surface anchor tagging.
- Check with runtime team (Ethan) about feasibility of attention-bias array in v1.1 API (impact on SDKs).

Random heuristics snippets I want to try in code:
- anchor_score = cosine(prefix_emb, anchor_emb) * min(1, anchor_age_days / 30)  # boost older anchors slowly
- eviction_priority = recency_score * 0.6 + anchor_use_count * 0.4  # prefer anchors with utility

Loose reading summary (one-liners):
- Contextual anchors are a cheap middle ground between full retrieval and naive prefix caching; main win is steering attention without large retrieval steps.
- Implementation within Redwood should prefer runtime-side biasing + cache tagging to avoid retraining and maintain compatibility with hosted/dedicated/private modes.

TODO (short):
- [ ] Prototype anchor-as-cache-entry (Me)
- [ ] Add anchor tag support to cache-service (Aisha)
- [ ] Runtime attention-bias spec + microbench (Ethan)
- [ ] Build small human eval sheet + recruit 30 raters

End notes / brain dump:
- Think about anchor lifespan tied to token drift: measure divergence of token distributions to decide when anchor should be refreshed.
- If experiments show consistent win, propose a "Anchor Mode" boolean in console with density tuning and cost estimate.

-- Mei

References mentioned above (quick):
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01234  "Contextual Anchors" (paper)
- https://github.com/redwood-inference/contextual-anchor-experiments/pull/17  PoC code
- CONFLUENCE-RA: ContextualAnchor/Overview  (internal brief)
